analysis.one_liner: Treats meat, poultry, and eggs carrying dangerous or antibiotic-resistant bacteria as adulterated and requires USDA testing.
analysis.headline: The food safety bill died in committee without a single cosponsor; it was referred to the House Agriculture Committee on December 19, 2018 and never moved before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the nation's meat, poultry, and egg inspection laws to declare products 'adulterated' — the legal trigger for keeping them out of commerce — if they carry bacteria linked to serious illness or death, or strains of Salmonella or Campylobacter that resist two or more antibiotics critically important for human medicine. The Department of Agriculture would have one year to build sampling and testing procedures to detect such products and stop them from reaching store shelves, with regulations due within 18 months. It was introduced in the final weeks of a Congress with no cosponsors and was never considered by the committee it was sent to.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers of meat, poultry, and eggs — essentially everyone who buys groceries. Foodborne bacteria like Salmonella and Campylobacter cause hundreds of thousands of illnesses a year, and antibiotic-resistant strains make those illnesses harder and sometimes impossible to treat with standard medicine. The bill would give USDA clear legal authority to keep contaminated products out of commerce rather than simply advising recalls.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Grocery shoppers and food safety advocates

how_it_helps.text: Redefines 'adulterated' under the Federal Meat Inspection Act, the Poultry Products Inspection Act, and the Egg Products Inspection Act to include microbial pathogens associated with serious illness or death, making it explicit that USDA can issue recalls of contaminated meat, poultry, and egg products.

Adds a new category of adulteration for products carrying strains of pathogens such as Salmonella or Campylobacter that are resistant to two or more antibiotics on the World Health Organization's list of critically important medicines for humans, addressed at the growing threat of drug-resistant foodborne illness.
Requires USDA, within one year of enactment, to establish sampling protocols and testing procedures to detect adulterated products and to prevent their entry into or movement in commerce.

analysis.who_pays: Meat, poultry, and egg processors, who would face new federal testing of their products and risk having batches declared adulterated and pulled from the market. Those compliance and recall costs would likely be passed partly to consumers through prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill would impose real costs on meat, poultry, and egg processors through mandatory sampling, testing, and recalls, and some of those costs would be passed to consumers as higher prices at the grocery store.

Classifying Salmonella and Campylobacter — bacteria that are widespread in raw poultry and can be killed by proper cooking — as adulterants is a contested policy choice; industry has long argued it could force the destruction of enormous quantities of otherwise conventional product and invite litigation, which is why USDA has historically regulated these pathogens through performance standards rather than the adulteration trigger.

The bill sets deadlines but leaves the hard technical choices — which technologies, how much sampling, what tolerance levels — entirely to USDA rulemaking, so its practical effect would depend heavily on how the department wrote the regulations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health upside is real: testing and a clear recall trigger for products carrying illness-causing or drug-resistant bacteria would remove contaminated food from the market before people get sick. The costs fall on processors and partly on grocery prices, and the design defers the difficult technical questions to USDA. Whether the trade is worth it depends on how strict the eventual testing rules would have been — but the bill was never debated, so that question was never answered in public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the last days of the 115th Congress and referred to the House Agriculture Committee, which never took it up before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the Pathogen Reduction and Testing Reform Act of 2018 on December 19, 2018, in the final weeks of the 115th Congress.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture, where it stayed.

No other member signed on as a cosponsor, and the committee took no further action on the bill before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, so it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meat, poultry, and egg processors avoided new testing requirements and recall exposure, and USDA kept the discretion it had — consumers got no added protection against drug-resistant foodborne pathogens.

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on December 19, 2018 and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had only one sponsor, so there was never a test of where the parties stood; the sole sponsor was a Democrat and no Republican or other Democrat signed on.

industries.note: The bill would subject their products to mandatory pathogen testing and could force recalls and destruction of product found to carry dangerous or drug-resistant bacteria. Those compliance costs and recall losses are the direct cost of keeping contaminated meat out of consumers' kitchens.
The bill extends the same adulteration and testing requirements to eggs, adding inspection and recall exposure for a smaller segment of the food supply.
The bill would require USDA to build and run new sampling and testing programs within a year, expanding the department's food safety role and the labs that support it.
